title: What is CI/CD and why it is essential
content:
Introduction: The DevOps revolution

CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) is not just a buzzword — it has become the indispensable standard of modern development. Before CI/CD, teams encountered recurring problems:
  • "It works on my machine" but explodes in prod
  • Manual integrations that take hours
  • Bugs discovered weeks after commit
  • Stressful Friday night deployments
CI/CD solves these problems by automating the entire cycle: from commit to production.

1️⃣ CI: Continuous Integration

Fundamental principle

Continuous integration is based on a simple concept: merge code frequently (multiple times a day) instead of waiting for weeks. With each commit or pull request, an automatic pipeline:
  • Clone code
  • Install dependencies
  • Launches the linting (ESLint, Prettier)
  • Runs unit and integration tests
  • Build the project
  • Checks code coverage
Objective: ensure that each commit leaves the project in a stable and deployable state.

Concrete example with GitHub Actions

File .github/workflows/ci.yml: ```yaml name: CI Pipeline on: push: branches: [ main, develop ] pull_request: branches: [ main ] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest strategy: matrix: node-version: [18, 20] steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Setup Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }} uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }} cache: 'npm' - name: Install dependencies run: npm ci - name: Lint code run: npm run lint - name: Run tests run: npm test -- --coverage - name: Build run: npm run build - name: Upload coverage to Codecov uses: codecov/codecov-action@v3 with: files: ./coverage/coverage-final.json ```

The benefits of CI

1. Immediate feedback You know in 5 minutes if your code breaks something, not 2 weeks later. 2. Fewer conflicts Frequent merges = smaller, easier to resolve Git conflicts. 3. Consistent quality Automatic testing prevents regressions from going to production. 4. Living documentation The pipeline itself documents the build process.

2️⃣ CD: Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment

Continuous Delivery

The code is still ready to deploy, but deployment to production requires manual validation. Typical workflow:
  • Code → CI → Build → Auto deployment on staging
  • Manual testing on staging
  • Manual click to deploy to production
Advantage: Human control before production (for critical features).

Continuous Deployment

Each commit that passes testing is automatically deployed to production without human intervention. Typical workflow:
  • Code → CI → Build → Auto-deploy staging → Auto-deploy production
Advantage: Maximum speed, multiple releases per day. Required: Very robust tests, feature flags, robust monitoring.

Example of CD with Vercel

```yaml deploy: needs: test runs-on: ubuntu-latest if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Deploy to Vercel Production uses: amondnet/vercel-action@v25 with: vercel-token: ${{ secrets.VERCEL_TOKEN }} vercel-org-id: ${{ secrets.ORG_ID }} vercel-project-id: ${{ secrets.PROJECT_ID }} vercel-args: '--prod' ```

3️⃣ Popular CI/CD tools

GitHub Actions

  • ✅ Free for public projects
  • ✅ Natively integrated with GitHub
  • ✅ Reusable Actions Marketplace
  • ❌ 2000 minutes/month on the free plan

GitLab CI/CD

  • ✅ Ultra-powerful pipeline
  • ✅ Auto DevOps (automatic language detection)
  • ✅ Self-hosted runners

CircleCI

  • ✅ Very fast (parallel builds)
  • ✅ Native Docker
  • ❌ Paying quickly

Jenkins

  • ✅ Open-source, very customizable
  • ✅ Thousands of plugins
  • ❌ Complex configuration
  • ❌ Requires dedicated server

4️⃣ The business benefits of CI/CD

1. Cost reduction Fewer bugs in prod = fewer emergency hotfixes = less overtime. 2. Accelerated time-to-market Deliver a feature in 1 day instead of 1 month. 3. Best Collaboration Devs, QA and ops share the same pipeline. 4. Quick customer feedback Test product hypotheses in just a few hours. 5. Increased confidence Deploying becomes mundane, more stressful.

5️⃣ Steps to implement CI/CD

Week 1: Basic CI

  • Set up unit tests
  • Configure a linter
  • Create a simple GitHub Actions workflow

Week 2: Improve CI

  • Add integration tests
  • Measure code coverage (>80%)
  • Test on multiple versions of Node

Week 3: CD on staging

  • Auto-deploy on a staging environment
  • Set up E2E tests (Playwright, Cypress)

Week 4: CD in production

  • Feature flags for phased deployments
  • Monitoring and alerts (Sentry, Datadog)
  • Automatic rollback on error

⚠️ Pitfalls to avoid

1. Pipeline too slow If the tests take 30 minutes, no one will wait for them. → Solution: parallelize, hide dependencies. 2. Flaky tests Tests that pass or fail randomly → loss of confidence. → Solution: avoid arbitrary timeouts, mock external APIs. 3. Deploy everything in direct production Even with the CD, maintains a staging environment. 4. Ignoring Secrets Never commit API keys → use encrypted secrets.

Conclusion

CI/CD is not an option — it is the foundation of a professional workflow. > “If it hurts, do it more often.” —Martin Fowler The more you deploy, the less risky it is. CI/CD transforms deployment from a stressful event into an everyday non-event. Next step: Set up your first GitHub Actions pipeline and feel the magic of seeing your tests pass automatically with every commit! 🚀

title: Set up a simple CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions
content:
Introduction: GitHub Actions, GitHub's native CI/CD

GitHub Actions has become the essential CI/CD tool for projects hosted on GitHub. Launched in 2019, it offers native integration with your repositories, eliminating the need to configure third-party services like Jenkins or Travis CI. The major advantage? Everything happens in one place: code, issues, pull requests and deployment pipelines.

1️⃣ Fundamental concepts

Workflows, Jobs and Steps

A workflow is an automated process defined in YAML and stored in .github/workflows/. Hierarchical structure:
  • Workflow: complete process (CI, CD, release...)
  • Job: execution unit (tests, build, deploy...)
  • Step: individual action (run command, use action...)

Triggers

GitHub Actions can react to many events:
  • push: on a commit
  • pull_request: opening/modifying PR
  • schedule: cron jobs (backups, cleanups...)
  • workflow_dispatch: manual trigger
  • release: creation of release

2️⃣ Full CI Pipeline

Create .github/workflows/ci.yml: ```yaml name: CI Pipeline on: push: branches: [main, develop] pull_request: branches: [main] jobs: lint: name: Code Quality runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Setup Node.js uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: '20' cache: 'npm' - run: npm ci - run: npm run lint - run: npm run format:check test: name: Tests runs-on: ubuntu-latest strategy: matrix: node-version: [18, 20] steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }} cache: 'npm' - run: npm ci - run: npm test -- --coverage - name: Upload coverage if: matrix.node-version == '20' uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4 with: token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }} build: name: Build needs: [lint, test] runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: '20' cache: 'npm' - run: npm ci - run: npm run build - name: Upload artifact uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 with: name: dist path: dist/ ```

Key points

1. Parallelization "lint" and "test" run at the same time. "build" expects their success with needs. 2. Matrix builds Testing on Node 18 and 20 simultaneously. 3. Caching cache: 'npm' divides the installation time by 3.

3️⃣ CD Pipeline: Deployment

.github/workflows/deploy.yml: ```yaml name: Deploy on: push: branches: [main] jobs: deploy-staging: name: Deploy Staging runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: name: staging url: https://staging.app.com steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: '20' cache: 'npm' - run: npm ci - run: npm run build env: VITE_API_URL: ${{ secrets.STAGING_API }} - name: Deploy to Vercel uses: amondnet/vercel-action@v25 with: vercel-token: ${{ secrets.VERCEL_TOKEN }} vercel-org-id: ${{ secrets.ORG_ID }} vercel-project-id: ${{ secrets.PROJECT_ID }} deploy-production: name: Deploy Production needs: deploy-staging runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: name: production url: https://app.com steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: '20' cache: 'npm' - run: npm ci - run: npm run build env: VITE_API_URL: ${{ secrets.PROD_API }} - name: Deploy to Vercel Prod uses: amondnet/vercel-action@v25 with: vercel-token: ${{ secrets.VERCEL_TOKEN }} vercel-org-id: ${{ secrets.ORG_ID }} vercel-project-id: ${{ secrets.PROJECT_ID }} vercel-args: '--prod' ```

4️⃣ Secret Management

Create secrets

In GitHub: Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions Types of secrets:
  • Repository secrets: accessible everywhere
  • Environment secrets: staging vs production
  • Organization secrets: shared between repos

Use in workflow

```yaml env: API_KEY: ${{ secrets.API_KEY }} DB_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }} PUBLIC_VAR: ${{ vars.PUBLIC_CONFIG }} ``` ⚠️ Security:
  • Never echo a secret
  • Automatically hide in logs
  • Revoke if compromised

5️⃣ Advanced optimizations

Multi-level caching

```yaml - name: Cache dependencies uses: actions/cache@v4 with: path: | ~/.npm node_modules .next/cache key: ${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }} ```

Conditional execution

```yaml - name: Deploy only on main if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && success() run: npm run deploy ```

Reusable workflows

Create reusable workflows to avoid duplication: ```yaml # .github/workflows/deploy-reusable.yml on: workflow_call: inputs: environment: required: true type: string ```

6️⃣ Marketplace Actions

Essential actions:
  • actions/checkout@v4: clone the repo
  • actions/setup-node@v4: installs Node.js
  • actions/cache@v4: cache dependencies
  • codecov/codecov-action: upload coverage
  • slackapi/slack-github-action: Slack notifications

7️⃣ Debugging

Enable detailed logs

Add in Settings → Secrets:
  • ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG = true
  • ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG = true

Show context

```yaml - name: Debug run: echo '${{ toJSON(github) }}' ```

8️⃣ Best Practices

1. Version actions
  • ✅ actions/checkout@v4
  • ❌ actions/checkout@main
2. Timeouts ```yaml jobs: test: timeout-minutes: 10 ``` 3. Fail fast ```yaml strategy: fail-fast: true ``` 4. Protected environments Enable “Required reviewers” for production.

🎯 Conclusion

GitHub Actions turns CI/CD into a transparent, automated process. Key benefits:
  • ✅ Free for public projects
  • ✅ Native GitHub integration
  • ✅ 10,000+ actions available
  • ✅ Simple configuration in YAML
Immediate Action: Create your first CI workflow today and watch the magic happen! 🚀 Resources:
  • docs.github.com/actions
  • github.com/marketplace?type=actions
  • github.com/sdras/awesome-actions

title: How to version effectively with Git and GitHub
content:
Introduction: Git, the developer's essential tool

Git is much more than just a versioning tool — it is the nervous system of any modern project. Mastering Git is the difference between a junior developer and a professional developer. Good versioning allows:
  • To collaborate effectively without overwriting the work of others
  • To keep a clean and navigable history
  • From go back at any time without panic
  • To deploy with confidence with traceable releases

1️⃣ Atomic commits and explicit messages

What is an atomic commit?

An atomic commit = a single logical change. Examples:
  • ✅ "fix: correct email validation regex"
  • ✅ "feat: add user authentication"
  • ❌ "update stuff" (too vague)
  • ❌ "fix login + add tests + update README" (3 different things)

Convention Conventional Commits

Standard format: type(scope): description Main types:
  • feat: new feature
  • fix: bug fix
  • docs: documentation only
  • style: formatting, missing semicolons (no code change)
  • refactor: refactoring (neither bug nor feature)
  • test: adding/modifying tests
  • chore: maintenance (dependencies, config...)
Concrete examples: ```bash feat(auth): add JWT token refresh mechanism fix(api): handle 404 errors in user endpoint docs(readme): update installation instructions refactor(utils): extract validation logic to separate module test(auth): add integration tests for login flow ```

2️⃣ Branch strategy

Git Flow vs GitHub Flow

GitHub Flow (recommended for most projects)
  • A branch main always deployable
  • Short feature branches: feature/feature-name
  • Pull Request → Review → Merge → Delete branch
Git Flow (for complex projects)
  • main: production
  • develop: integration
  • feature/*: new features
  • release/*: release preparation
  • hotfix/*: urgent fixes in production

Branch naming

Clear conventions:
  • feature/user-authentication
  • bugfix/fix-email-validation
  • hotfix/critical-security-patch
  • chore/update-dependencies
❌ Avoid: test, dev, john-branch

3️⃣ Daily Git Workflow

Start a new feature

```bash # Mettre à jour main git checkout main git pull origin main # Créer une branche de feature git checkout -b feature/payment-integration # Travailler... git add src/payment/ git commit -m "feat(payment): add Stripe integration" # Pousser la branche git push -u origin feature/payment-integration ```

Synchronize with main during development

```bash # Récupérer les dernières modifications de main git checkout main git pull origin main # Rebaser votre branche sur main git checkout feature/payment-integration git rebase main # Si conflits : résoudre, puis git add . git rebase --continue # Forcer le push (après rebase) git push --force-with-lease ``` ⚠️ Tip: Use --force-with-lease instead of --force to avoid overwriting someone else's work.

4️⃣ Professional Pull Requests

PR template

Example of full description:
  • Description: Added Stripe integration for payments
  • Type: New feature
  • Checklist: Tests added, Documentation updated, Build CI passes
  • Tests: Payment of €10 made successfully

Best practices for reviews

For the author:
  • Short PR (<400 lignes modifiées)
  • Clear description of "why"
  • Automatic tests passing
  • Screenshots if UI modified
For the reviewer:
  • Constructive and caring feedback
  • Questions to understand the context
  • Suggestions with code examples
  • Approve if it's "good enough", not perfect

5️⃣ Semantic versioning (SemVer)

Format: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH

Example: 2.4.1
  • MAJOR (2): incompatible change (breaking change)
  • MINOR (4): new backwards compatible feature
  • PATCH (1): backwards compatible bug fix

Create a release on GitHub

```bash # Tagger une version git tag -a v2.4.1 -m "Release 2.4.1: Fix payment bug" git push origin v2.4.1 ``` On GitHub: Releases → Draft new release

6️⃣ .gitignore and sensitive files

Files to always ignore

```gitignore # Dépendances node_modules/ vendor/ # Fichiers de build dist/ build/ .next/ # Variables d'environnement .env .env.local .env.production # IDE .vscode/ .idea/ *.swp # OS .DS_Store Thumbs.db # Logs logs/ *.log npm-debug.log* ``` ⚠️ Crucial: NEVER commit API keys, passwords or tokens.

7️⃣ Useful Advanced Git Commands

Squash of commits

```bash # Squash les 3 derniers commits git rebase -i HEAD~3 # Dans l'éditeur, remplacer 'pick' par 'squash' ou 's' # Sauvegarder et écrire un nouveau message de commit ```

Cherry-pick a specific commit

```bash git cherry-pick abc1234 ```

Temporary stash

```bash # Mettre de côté les modifications git stash save "WIP: feature en cours" # Lister les stash git stash list # Récupérer le stash git stash pop ```

View file history

```bash git log --follow -p -- src/auth/login.ts ```

8️⃣ Branch protection on GitHub

Recommended protection rules

In Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules:
  • ✅ Require pull request before merging
  • ✅ Require approvals (1-2)
  • ✅ Require status checks to pass (CI/CD)
  • ✅ Require conversation resolution
  • ✅ Include administrators
  • ❌ Allow force pushes (disable)

🎯 Conclusion

Clean Git versioning is not a luxury — it is the mark of a professional developer. Golden rules:
  • Atomic commits with clear messages
  • Short, focused branches
  • Well-documented pull requests
  • hand still stable and deployable
  • Never secrets in the code
Resources:
  • conventionalcommits.org
  • gitflow.github.io
  • semver.org
  • github.com/github/gitignore (templates)
> "A clean Git history tells the story of your project. Make it readable." 📖

title: Common Git errors and how to avoid them
content:
Introduction: Even the best make mistakes

Git is powerful, but with that power comes the classic pitfalls that every developer encounters. The good news? Every Git error has a solution.

1️⃣ Committed to the wrong branch

❌ The problem

You code a feature on main instead of creating a dedicated branch.

✅ The solution (if not yet pushed)

  • Stash your changes: git stash
  • Create the correct branch: git checkout -b feature/my-feature
  • Apply your changes: git stash pop
  • Clean main: git checkout main && git reset --hard origin/main

✅ Alternative (if already committed)

  • git branch feature/my-feature (create branch from current commit)
  • git reset --hard HEAD~1 (backtrack to main)
  • git checkout feature/my-feature

2️⃣ Failed conflict merge

❌ The problem

You run a git merge and everything goes into a tailspin with conflicts everywhere.

✅ Cancel the current merge

  • git merge --abort (return to the state before the merge)

✅ Better: Use rebase instead of merge

Rebase replays your commits above the target branch, often avoiding conflicts:
  • git checkout feature/my-feature
  • git pull origin main --rebase
  • Resolve conflicts one by one
  • git rebase --continue

🎯 Prevention

  • Always pull before merge
  • Regularly synchronize your branch with main
  • Uses small PRs to reduce conflicts

3️⃣ Loss of commits

❌ The problem

You did a git reset --hard or deleted a branch, and your commits disappeared.

✅ Recovery with reflog

Git keeps a history of all your actions (for 30 days by default):
  • git reflog (see HEAD history)
  • Find the SHA of the lost commit (ex: abc1234)
  • git cherry-pick abc1234 (get this commit)
  • Or: git checkout abc1234 then git checkout -b recovery-branch

💡 Tip

Git almost never forgets. Even after a --hard reset, reflog saves you.

4️⃣ Commit sensitive files (.env, secrets)

❌ The problem

You committed a file .env with API keys or passwords.

✅ Remove file from history

  • git rm --cached .env (remove from Git tracker)
  • Add .env to .gitignore
  • git commit -m "chore: remove .env from tracking"

⚠️ If already pushed to GitHub

CRITICAL ALERT: Your secrets are public.
  • Immediately revoke all exposed keys
  • Clean history with git filter-branch or BFG Repo-Cleaner
  • Force push: git push --force
  • Notify your team to re-clone the repo

5️⃣ Unreadable history with too many commits

❌ The problem

You have 50 commits "fix typo", "wip", "test"...

✅ Squash before merge

Combine multiple commits into one:
  • git rebase -i HEAD~5 (interactive on the last 5 commits)
  • Replace pick with squash (or s) for commits to merge
  • Save and write a new clean commit message
  • git push --force-with-lease

📊 View History

  • git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
  • Or use GitKraken, SourceTree or the Git extension Graph in VSCode

6️⃣ Force destructive push

❌ The problem

You do git push --force and you overwrite someone else's work.

✅ Use --force-with-lease

  • git push --force-with-lease
This verifies that no one has pushed in the meantime. If so, the push is rejected.

🎯 Golden rule

NEVER force push on main or develop (uses branch protection on GitHub).

7️⃣ Forgetting to pull before pushing

❌ The problem

You push and Git refuses: "Updates were rejected because the remote contains work..."

✅ Solution

  • git pull --rebase origin main
  • Resolve possible conflicts
  • git push

🎯 Automation

Configure an alias:
  • git config --global alias.sync 'pull --rebase'
  • Then: git sync

🛡️ Good habits to avoid mistakes

  • ✅ Always pull before starting a feature
  • ✅ Create a branch for each change
  • ✅ Short and frequent commits (atomic)
  • ✅ Use .gitignore from the start of the project
  • ✅ Never commit secrets (.env, tokens, passwords)
  • ✅ Use --force-with-lease instead of --force
  • ✅ Enable branch protection on main

🚨 Fallback Commands

Undo local changes

  • git restore . (revert all modified files)
  • git restore src/file.ts (undo specific file)

Revert last commit (but keep changes)

  • git reset --soft HEAD~1

Revert last commit (and DELETE changes)

  • git reset --hard HEAD~1

See who modified a row

  • git blame src/file.ts

🎯 Conclusion

Git may seem intimidating, but every error is reversible. The keys:
  • Understanding reflog (your safety net)
  • Never panic: Git almost never forgets
  • Use branches and atomic commits
  • Protect main with branch protection rules
Resources:
  • ohshitgit.com (humorous troubleshooting guide)
  • dangitgit.com (version without swear words)
  • git-scm.com/book (official documentation)
> "Git is hard: screwing up is easy, and figuring out how to fix your mistakes is tough. But don't worry — you got this!" 🚀

title: Docker for beginners: understanding images, containers and volumes
content:
Introduction: Docker, the portability revolution

Docker allows you to run your code "everywhere in the same way". It is one of the pillars of modern DevOps and the solution to the famous “It works on my machine!”. Docker solves a universal problem: ensuring that your app runs identically on your PC, the staging server and production.

🐳 What is Docker?

Docker is a containerization platform that packs your application with all its dependencies into a lightweight, portable unit called container.

Difference with a VM

  • Virtual Machine: Emulates a complete OS (heavy, slow)
  • Docker Container: Shares the host kernel (light, fast)
A Docker container starts in a few milliseconds vs several minutes for a VM.

1️⃣ The 3 fundamental concepts

📦 Docker Image

An image is an immutable template which contains:
  • A minimal operating system (Alpine, Ubuntu...)
  • Your runtime (Node.js, Python, Java...)
  • Your dependencies
  • Your application code
Think of an image as a cooking recipe: it describes how to build the environment.

🏃 Container Docker

A container is a running instance of an image. Analogy: if the image is the recipe, the container is the cooked dish. You can launch several containers from the same image (like making several cakes with the same recipe).

💾 Docker Volume

A volume is a persistent storage that survives the deletion of the container. Why is this crucial? Because containers are ephemeral: when you delete a container, all its internal data disappears. The volumes make it possible to:
  • Persist database data
  • Share files between containers
  • Separate data from code

2️⃣ Create your first Docker image

The Dockerfile

The Dockerfile is the configuration file that defines how to build your image. Example for a Node.js app: Instructions explained:
  • FROM node:20-alpine: Base image (Node 20 on Alpine Linux, super light 40 MB)
  • WORKDIR /app: Working directory in the container
  • COPY package*.json ./: Copy dependency files first (cache optimization)
  • RUN npm ci: Install dependencies (npm ci = faster and deterministic than npm install)
  • COPY . .: Copy all source code
  • EXPOSE 3000: Document port (informational only)
  • CMD: Command executed when starting the container

Build image

  • docker build -t my-app .
The option -t gives a name (tag) to your image.

3️⃣ Launch a container

Basic command

  • docker run -p 3000:3000 my-app
-p 3000:3000: Map port 3000 of the container to port 3000 of your PC

Useful options

  • -d: Detached mode (background)
  • --name my-container: Give a name to the container
  • -e VAR=value: Pass an environment variable
  • -v /host/path:/container/path: Mount a volume
  • --rm: Delete the container automatically after shutdown
Complete example:
  • docker run -d --name api -p 5000:5000 -e NODE_ENV=production my-app

4️⃣ Manage volumes

Create a volume named

  • docker volume create my-data

Use volume in container

  • docker run -v my-data:/app/data my-app
Data written to /app/data in the container will be persisted in the volume.

Bind mount (map local folder)

  • docker run -v $(pwd):/app my-app
Useful for hot reload in development.

5️⃣ Essential Docker Commands

Container management

  • docker ps: List current containers
  • docker ps -a: All containers (even stopped)
  • docker stop : Stop a container
  • docker start : Restart a stopped container
  • docker rm : Delete a container
  • docker logs : View logs
  • docker exec -it sh: Open a shell in the container

Image management

  • docker images: List images
  • docker rmi : Delete an image
  • docker pull : Download an image from Docker Hub
  • docker push : Push an image to a registry

Cleaning

  • docker system prune: Clean up anything unused
  • docker system prune -a --volumes: Aggressive cleanup (delete all)

6️⃣ Best practices

  • ✅ Uses Alpine images (lighter)
  • ✅ Multi-stage builds to reduce the final size
  • ✅ .dockerignore to exclude node_modules, .git, etc.
  • ✅ Do not run as root (security)
  • ✅ Copy package.json before code (cache optimization)
  • ✅ One process per container (Unix principle)

7️⃣ Concrete use cases

Local dev identical to prod

No more “it works on my machine”: everyone uses the same container.

Automated CI/CD

Build an image, test it, deploy it. Same artifact from dev to production.

Project isolation

Project A with Node 18, Project B with Node 20? No conflict.

🎯 Conclusion

Docker is the key to modern portability. The 3 concepts to remember:
  • Image: Immutable template
  • Container: Running instance
  • Volume: Data persistence
You code on your PC, you deploy on any server. Build once, run anywhere. Resources:
  • docs.docker.com
  • hub.docker.com (official images)
  • dockerlabs.collabnix.com
> "Docker solved the 'works on my machine' problem forever." 🐳

title: Create your dev environment with Docker Compose
content:
Introduction: Multi-service orchestration made simple

Docker Compose allows you to manage multiple services (database, API, frontend, Redis, etc.) in a single command. Finish throwing 10 terminals to start your stack. With Compose, docker compose up and everything starts.

🎯 What is Docker Compose?

Docker Compose is a local orchestration tool that allows you to define and manage multi-container applications via a YAML file. A single docker-compose.yml file for your entire local infrastructure.

1️⃣ Concrete example: Stack MERN

Project structure

  • frontend/: React app
  • backend/: Node.js API
  • mongo: MongoDB database
  • redis: Cache

Complete docker-compose.yml file

Detailed explanations:
  • services: Each defined container (frontend, backend, mongo, redis)
  • build: Build the image from a local Dockerfile
  • ports: Map container ports → host
  • environment: Environment variables
  • depends_on: Startup order (backend waits for mongo)
  • volumes: Data persistence + hot reload code
  • networks: Internal communication between services

2️⃣ Essential Docker Compose Commands

Start all services

  • docker compose up: Launch in foreground (logs visible)
  • docker compose up -d: Detached mode (background)
  • docker compose up --build: Rebuild the images before launching

Stop and clean

  • docker compose down: Stop and delete containers
  • docker compose down -v: Also delete the volumes (WARNING: lost data)
  • docker compose stop: Stop without removing
  • docker compose start: Restart stopped containers

Management of individual services

  • docker compose logs backend: View the logs of a service
  • docker compose logs -f: Track logs in real time
  • docker compose exec backend sh: Open a shell in a service
  • docker compose restart backend: Restart a specific service

Rebuild and clean

  • docker compose build: Rebuild the images without launching
  • docker compose build --no-cache: Rebuild from scratch
  • docker compose ps: List running services

3️⃣ Environment variables

Use .env file

Creates a file .env at the root: Example: DB_USER=admin, DB_PASSWORD=secret123, REDIS_PORT=6379 In docker-compose.yml, reference them with ${DB_USER}

⚠️ Security

  • Add .env to .gitignore
  • Creates an .env.example with dummy values for team

4️⃣ Volumes: Data persistence vs Hot Reload

Named volume (persistence)

Data survives docker compose down.

Bind mount (hot reload)

Local code changes immediately reflected in the container.

5️⃣ Networking: Inter-service communication

By default, Compose creates a bridge network where all services can communicate. Example: from the backend, you can do fetch('http://redis:6379') — the service name becomes the hostname.

6️⃣ Best Practices

  • ✅ One docker-compose.yml per environment (dev, staging, prod)
  • ✅ Uses .env for secrets
  • ✅ Do not commit .env
  • ✅ Healthchecks for dependencies (ex: wait for Postgres to be ready)
  • ✅ Named volumes for DBs (avoids data loss)
  • ✅ Restart policies : restart: unless-stopped

7️⃣ Advanced use cases

Profiles (launch only specific services)

Launch only the backend and the DB, without the front:
  • docker compose --profile backend up

Override file

docker-compose.override.yml for specific local configurations.

8️⃣ Debugging

Service not starting?

  • Check logs: docker compose logs backend
  • Inspect the container: docker compose ps
  • Rebuild: docker compose up --build

Port already in use?

  • Change host port: "3001:3000"

🎯 Conclusion

Docker Compose is your indispensable local orchestrator. Key benefits:
  • Unique configuration for the entire team
  • Easy to replicate in staging or production
  • No need to install dependencies locally (MongoDB, Redis...)
  • Hot reload for dev
Resources:
  • docs.docker.com/compose
  • github.com/compose-spec/compose-spec
  • awesome-compose (example stacks)
> "Docker Compose: because nobody wants to run 10 terminal tabs to start an app." 🚀

title: Best practices for staging and production environments
content:
Introduction: The golden rule of professional deployment

A professional project must always have at least three environments:
  • Dev: to code and experiment
  • Staging: to test in real conditions
  • Production: to deliver to users
NEVER test directly in production — this is the mark of an amateur developer.

1️⃣ Why separate environments?

❌ Risks without staging

  • Critical bug discovered in production after deployment
  • DB migration that breaks everything
  • Feature incompatible with production
  • Catastrophic performance under real load

✅ Advantages of a staging environment

  • Test in real conditions before production
  • QA can validate without risk
  • Client demo on a stable environment
  • Fast rollback if problem detected

2️⃣ Architecture of the 3 environments

🛠️ Dev (Development)

  • Goal: Code, experiment, debug
  • Infrastructure: Local (Docker Compose) or cloud (minimal resources)
  • Database: Local or shared between devs
  • Deployment: Manual or auto on push (feature branches)
  • Logs: Verbous (debug mode)

🔍 Staging (Pre-production)

  • But: Test in conditions identical to production
  • Infrastructure: Clone of the production (same OS, same versions)
  • Database: Anonymized copy of the production
  • Deployment: Auto on merge in develop or staging branch
  • Logs: Production mode
  • Monitoring: Enabled (same tools as in production)

🚀 Production

  • Goal: Serve real users
  • Infrastructure: Optimized for performance and resiliency
  • Database: Real data (GDPR, frequent backups)
  • Deployment: Manual with approval or auto on hand with tests
  • Monitoring: 24/7 with alerts
  • Access: Restricted (admins only)

3️⃣ Environment variables

Principle: Outsourced configuration

NEVER hardcode configs in code.

Example of .env by environment

Dev (.env.development) Staging (.env.staging) Production (.env.production)

🎯 Secret management

  • Dev: local .env (uncommitted)
  • Staging/Prod: Env variables in Vercel, Railway, AWS Secrets Manager, etc.
  • Use dotenv (Node) or equivalents

4️⃣ Database by environment

⚠️ Classic error

Share the same DB between dev and prod → CATASTROPHE GUARANTEED.

✅ Good practice

  • Dev: Local DB (Docker Postgres/MongoDB)
  • Staging: isolated cloud DB with anonymized copy of the production
  • Production: DB protected with daily backups

Migration scripts

Use tools like Prisma, TypeORM, Alembic for versioned migrations.

5️⃣ Git Workflow

Branch policy

  • feature/* → Dev environment (optional auto-deploy)
  • develop → Staging environment (auto-deploy)
  • main → Production environment (deploy manually or with approval)

CI/CD Pipeline

  • Push on develop → Tests → Deploy staging
  • Merge into main → Tests → Approval → Deploy prod

6️⃣ Monitoring and observability

Staging: Like production

  • Same monitoring tools (Datadog, New Relic, Sentry)
  • Structured logs
  • Alerts (but without paging the team at 3 a.m.)

Production: 24/7 monitoring

  • Uptime monitoring: UptimeRobot, Pingdom
  • Error tracking: Sentry, Rollbar
  • Performance: Lighthouse CI, Web Vitals
  • Logs: CloudWatch, Logtail, Loki

7️⃣ Feature Flags

Why?

Enable/disable features without redeploying.

Example with LaunchDarkly or custom

  • Feature activated in staging for tests
  • Feature disabled in production until validation
  • Progressive rollout (5% users → 50% → 100%)

8️⃣ Security and access

Access control

  • Dev: All devs
  • Staging: Devs + QA + Product
  • Production: Admins only (principle of least privilege)

Secret Protection

  • Use AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault
  • Automatic API key rotation
  • Audit logs to trace access

9️⃣ Recommended tools

  • Docker Compose: Identical stacks between env
  • Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
  • GitHub Actions: CI/CD pipeline
  • Vercel/Railway: Preview automatic deployments
  • Doppler/Infisical: Centralized management of secrets

🎯 Conclusion

Good DevOps never tests directly in production. Golden rules:
  • At least 3 environments (Dev, Staging, Prod)
  • Externalized env variables (never hardcoded secrets)
  • Separate databases
  • Staging = prod clone
  • Monitoring enabled everywhere
  • Restricted access to production
> "Test in staging like it's production. Treat production like it's sacred." 🛡️

title: Introduction to Kubernetes (for the curious)
content:
Introduction: The container orchestrator

Kubernetes (or K8s) is a container orchestration tool that automates the deployment, scaling, and resiliency of your applications. If Docker is your container runtime, Kubernetes is your conductor that manages hundreds of containers.

🤔 Why Kubernetes?

Issues K8s Fixes

  • Manual scaling: K8s scales automatically depending on the load
  • App crashes: Self-healing (auto restart of pods)
  • Risky deployments: Rolling updates without downtime
  • Load balancing: Automatic traffic distribution
  • Secrets management: Native ConfigMaps and Secrets

1️⃣ Kubernetes Architecture

Control Plane (brain)

  • API Server: Entry point for all commands
  • Scheduler: Decides where to place the pods
  • Controller Manager: Maintains the desired state
  • etcd: Key-value database (stores cluster state)

Nodes (workers)

  • Kubelet: Agent on each node that runs the pods
  • Kube-proxy: Manages the network
  • Container Runtime: Docker, containerd...

2️⃣ Key concepts

📦 Pod

The base unit in K8s. A pod contains 1 or more containers that share:
  • The same IP
  • The same storage (volumes)
  • The same network namespace
Generally: 1 pod = 1 main container.

🚀 Deployment

Manages the pod lifecycle:
  • Number of replicas (scalability)
  • Rolling updates (progressive deployments)
  • Automatic rollback if failure

🌐 Service

Expose your pods to the network with a stable IP. Types:
  • ClusterIP: Accessible only in cluster
  • NodePort: Exposes on a port of node
  • LoadBalancer: Creates an external load balancer (AWS ELB, GCP LB...)

🔀 Ingress

Manages external HTTP/HTTPS access with intelligent routing. Example: api.example.com → backend service, example.com → frontend service

3️⃣ Complete example: Deploy an app

Deployment (deployment.yaml)

Explanations:
  • replicas: 3: 3 identical pods (high availability)
  • selector: Identifies the pods to manage
  • template: Defines the pod
  • image: The Docker image to use

Service (service.yaml)

Expose the pods with a load balancer.

kubectl commands

  • kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml: Deploy
  • kubectl get pods: List pods
  • kubectl logs pod-name: View logs
  • kubectl exec -it pod-name -- sh: Shell in pod
  • kubectl scale deployment webapp --replicas=5: Scaler

4️⃣ Auto-scaling

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)

Automatically scale according to CPU/RAM:
  • kubectl autoscale deployment webapp --cpu-percent=50 --min=2 --max=10
If CPU > 50%, K8s adds pods (up to 10 max).

5️⃣ ConfigMaps and Secrets

ConfigMap (non-sensitive configuration)

Example: API URL, environment name.

Secret (sensitive data)

Example: Passwords, API tokens (base64 encoded).

6️⃣ When to use Kubernetes?

✅ YES if:

  • Many microservices (>10 services)
  • Need for strong and automatic scalability
  • Dedicated DevOps team
  • Multi-cloud or hybrid cloud

❌ NO if:

  • Small project / simple monolith
  • No DevOps resources (learning curve)
  • Serverless is enough (Lambda, Cloud Functions)
  • Docker Compose meets your needs

7️⃣ Alternatives and managed solutions

  • Amazon EKS: Kubernetes managed on AWS
  • Google GKE: Kubernetes managed on GCP
  • Azure AKS: Kubernetes managed on Azure
  • Minikube: local K8s for dev
  • K3s: Lightweight version for IoT/Edge

🎯 Conclusion

Kubernetes is a very large-scale Docker Compose. Advantages:
  • Auto scaling
  • High availability
  • Centralized resource management
  • Industry standard
Not essential for beginners, but essential to master in the long term. Resources:
  • kubernetes.io/docs
  • learnk8s.io
  • kubernetes.io/training
> "Kubernetes: because manually managing 100 Docker containers is insane." ☸️

title: Automate tests before deployment
content:
Introduction: The CI/CD Safety Net

Automating tests means guaranteeing that each production release is done without surprises. This is the basis of a quality pipeline. Without automated tests:
  • Critical bug discovered in production after deployment
  • Undetected regression (feature that breaks another)
  • Risky refactoring (fear of breaking everything)
With automated tests:
  • Immediate feedback (failure = blocked pipeline)
  • Confidence to refactor
  • Living code documentation

1️⃣ The testing pyramid

🔬 Unit Tests (70% of tests)

Objective: Check isolated functions/methods. Features:
  • Ultra fast (milliseconds)
  • No external dependencies (DB, API)
  • Many (hundreds of tests)
Example with Jest (JavaScript): Tests pure logic without side effects.

🔗 Integration Tests (20% of tests)

Objective: Validate communication between modules. Example: Test an API that actually queries a test DB. Tools: Supertest (Node), pytest (Python)

🎭 End-to-End (E2E) Tests (10% of tests)

Objective: Simulate full user behavior. Example: Test the “Login → Create a post → Logout” flow in a real browser. Tools: Playwright, Cypress, Selenium

2️⃣ Integrate tests into CI/CD

GitHub Actions: Full Pipeline

Workflow steps:
  • Code checkout
  • Installing dependencies
  • Linting (ESLint, Prettier)
  • Unit tests
  • Integration tests
  • Build
  • E2E tests (optional)
If only one test fails, the pipeline stops → no deployment.

GitLab CI equivalent

Same principle with .gitlab-ci.yml.

3️⃣ Code Coverage: Measuring quality

What is code coverage?

Percentage of code tested by the tests.
  • 80% coverage = good
  • 90%+ = excellent
  • 100% = unrealistic (and not always useful)

Generate a report with Jest

  • npm test -- --coverage
Shows: lines, branches, functions, statements covered.

Enforce a minimum threshold

In package.json or jest.config.js: The build fails if coverage < 80%.

4️⃣ Non-regression tests

Problem: Refactoring that breaks

You change code → an existing feature stops working.

Solution: Automated tests

Each fixed bug must have an associated test to prevent it from coming back. Workflow:
  • Bug discovered in production
  • Write a test that fails (reproduces the bug)
  • Fix bug
  • Test passes → commit

5️⃣ Performance Tests

Lighthouse CI

Test the Web Vitals with each commit:
  • Performance (LCP, FID, CLS)
  • Accessibility
  • SEO
  • Best practices

Load testing

Tools: k6, Artillery, JMeter Simulate 1000 concurrent users to test scalability.

6️⃣ Best practices

  • ✅ Quick tests: Unitary < 1s, Intégration < 10s
  • ✅ Deterministic tests: No flaky tests (which fail randomly)
  • ✅ A test = a clear assertion: Easy to debug
  • ✅ Reasonable coverage: 80% is a good objective
  • ✅ Isolated tests: No dependencies between tests
  • ✅ Fail fast: Stop the pipeline on the first failure

7️⃣ Tools by language

JavaScript/TypeScript

  • Jest: Unit/integration testing
  • Vitest: Ultra-fast alternative
  • Playwright: E2E Tests
  • Cypress: E2E tests (simpler)

Python

  • pytest: Test framework
  • unittest: Integrated with Python
  • Selenium: E2E Tests

Java

  • JUnit: Standard for unit tests
  • Mockito: Mocking

8️⃣ TDD: Test-Driven Development

Principle

Write tests BEFORE code. Cycle:
  • 🔴 Red: Write a test that fails
  • 🟢 Green: Write the minimum code to make it pass
  • 🔵 Refactor: Improve the code without breaking the test

Benefits

  • Testable code from the start
  • Better architecture (decoupling)
  • Confidence to refactor

🎯 Conclusion

Self-tests are the CI/CD bumper. Without them, your pipeline is a highway without brakes. Golden rules:
  • Pipeline blocked if tests fail
  • Minimum coverage: 80%
  • Fast and deterministic tests
  • Test pyramid respected (70% unit, 20% integ, 10% E2E)
Resources:
  • jestjs.io
  • playwright.dev
  • martinfowler.com/testing
> "Code without tests is broken by design." —Jacob Kaplan-Moss 🧪

title: Monitor and monitor your apps after deployment
content:
Introduction: Observability, the key to reliability

Delivering is good. Observe, is better. An app without monitoring is a plane without a dashboard. Questions that monitoring should answer:
  • Is my app accessible? (Uptime)
  • Is it fast? (Performance)
  • Are there any errors? (Error tracking)
  • Are the resources healthy? (CPU, RAM, Disk)

1️⃣ The 3 pillars of observability

📝 Logs (what happened)

Definition: Timestamped records of events. Example:
  • 2025-01-10 14:32:15 INFO User 123 logged in
  • 2025-01-10 14:35:42 ERROR Database connection failed
Log levels:
  • DEBUG: Details for dev (disabled in prod)
  • INFO: Normal events
  • WARN: Potential problem
  • ERROR: Recoverable error
  • CRITICAL: Critical error (system down)

📊 Metrics (what happens in real time)

Definition: Numerical values measured over time. Examples:
  • CPU usage: 45%
  • RAM: 2.3 GB / 8 GB
  • Requests per second: 1200
  • Response time: 230ms
  • Error rate: 0.5%

🔍 Traces (travel of a query)

Definition: Tracking the path of a request through all services. Example: User request → API Gateway → Auth Service → Database → Response Tools: Jaeger, Zipkin, OpenTelemetry

2️⃣ Complete monitoring stack

📝 Logs: ELK Stack

Components:
  • Elasticsearch: Storage and indexing of logs
  • Logstash: Collection and transformation
  • Kibana: Visualization (dashboards)
Modern alternative: Loki + Grafana (lighter)

📊 Metrics: Prometheus + Grafana

Prometheus:
  • Time-series database (stores metrics over time)
  • Pull model (scrape endpoints /metrics)
  • Integrated alert
Grafana:
  • Beautiful dashboards
  • Visual alert
  • Multi-sources (Prometheus, Loki, InfluxDB...)

🚨 Error Tracking: Sentry

Automatically captures exceptions and errors in prod. Features:
  • Full stack traces
  • User context (browser, OS, user ID)
  • Source maps (JS errors deminified)
  • Slack/Email Alerts

⏱️ Uptime Monitoring

Tools:
  • UptimeRobot: Free, ping every 5 min
  • Pingdom: Advanced monitoring
  • Better Uptime: Status page + alerting

3️⃣ Configure Prometheus + Grafana

Step 1: Expose the metrics

Node.js example with prom-client: Exposes an endpoint /metrics that Prometheus scrapes.

Step 2: Configure Prometheus

In prometheus.yml:

Step 3: Create a Grafana dashboard

  • Add Prometheus as a data source
  • Create a dashboard with panels (CPU, RAM, Requests/s...)
  • Configure alerts (CPU > 80%)

4️⃣ Intelligent alerting

When to alert?

  • 🔴 Critical: Site down, DB inaccessible → Immediate alert (SMS, call)
  • 🟠 Warning: CPU > 80%, Disk > 90% → Slack/Email
  • 🟡 Info: Deploy successful → Log only

Avoid fatigue alert

Problem: Too many alerts → we ignore them. Solution:
  • Alert only on what requires immediate action
  • Group similar alerts
  • Silence during maintenance

5️⃣ Performance Monitoring

Web Vitals (Frontend)

Google Metrics:
  • LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): Loading time of main content
  • FID (First Input Delay): Responsiveness to clicks
  • CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift): Visual stability
Tools:
  • Google Analytics 4
  • Vercel Analytics
  • web-vitals library

APM (Application Performance Monitoring)

Tools:
  • Datadog APM: Distributed traces
  • New Relic: All-in-one monitoring
  • Elastic APM: Integrated with ELK

6️⃣ Structured logs

JSON Logs

Instead of: "User 123 logged in at 2:32 p.m." Prefer: Easier to parse and index in Elasticsearch.

7️⃣ Best practices

  • ✅ Centralize logs (ELK, Loki)
  • ✅ Alert on critical thresholds (CPU > 90%, errors > 1%)
  • ✅ Clear Dashboards (Grafana)
  • ✅ Retention policy (delete old logs to save)
  • ✅ Monitoring monitoring (Prometheus monitoring Prometheus)
  • ✅ Connect to CI/CD (alert on deploy failed)

8️⃣ All-in-one solutions

  • Datadog: Logs + Metrics + APM + Tracing (paid but powerful)
  • New Relic: Complete monitoring (generous free tier)
  • Grafana Cloud: Loki + Prometheus + Grafana managed
  • AWS CloudWatch: Native AWS
  • Azure Monitor: Native Azure

🎯 Conclusion

Good DevOps never sleeps peacefully without a dashboard. To monitor is to control. The 3 pillars:
  • Logs (what happened)
  • Metrics (what's happening)
  • Traces (request traversal)
Resources:
  • prometheus.io
  • grafana.com
  • sentry.io/welcome
  • opentelemetry.io
> "You can't improve what you don't measure." —Peter Drucker 📊

title: Infrastructure as Code with Terraform
content:
Introduction: Managing infrastructure like code

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) = Define your cloud infrastructure in versioned files. Before IaC:
  • Manual clicks in AWS Console
  • Outdated Word Documentation
  • Unable to reproduce
With IaC:
  • Versioned code in Git
  • Infinitely reproducible
  • Infra review code

🏗️ Terraform: The IaC standard

Why Terraform?

  • Multi-cloud: AWS, Azure, GCP, DigitalOcean...
  • Declarative: You describe the final state, Terraform does the rest
  • Plan before apply: Preview of changes before execution
  • State management: Knows the current vs desired state
  • Immutability: Replaces instead of modifying

Alternatives

  • Pulumi: IaC with TypeScript/Python/Go
  • AWS CloudFormation: AWS specific (YAML/JSON)
  • Azure ARM Templates: Azure specific
  • Ansible: Configuration management (rather imperative)

2️⃣ First example: EC2 instance

Main.tf file

```hcl provider "aws" { region = "eu-west-1" } resource "aws_instance" "web" { ami = "ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0" instance_type = "t2.micro" tags = { Name = "WebServer" Environment = "Production" } } ``` Explanations:
  • provider: Configures AWS (region, credentials)
  • resource: Creates a resource (here an EC2 server)
  • ami: System image (Amazon Linux, Ubuntu...)
  • instance_type: Server size (t2.micro = 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM)
  • tags: Metadata to organize

Terraform Workflow

  • terraform init: Download the providers (AWS, Azure...)
  • terraform plan: See what will be created/modified/destroyed
  • terraform apply: Apply changes (request confirmation)
  • terraform destroy: Destroy everything (cleanup)

3️⃣ Variables and outputs

Variables (variables.tf)

Make the code reusable: ```hcl variable "region" { default = "eu-west-1" } variable "instance_type" { default = "t2.micro" } ``` Usage: var.region, var.instance_type

Outputs (outputs.tf)

Show info after apply: ```hcl output "instance_ip" { value = aws_instance.web.public_ip } ``` Shows the public IP of the created server.

4️⃣ Reusable modules

Why modules?

Instead of duplicating code, wraps it into modules. Structure example:
  • modules/vpc/ (Virtual Private Cloud)
  • modules/ec2/ (Servers)
  • modules/rds/ (Database)

Using a module

```hcl module "vpc" { source = "./modules/vpc" cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16" environment = "production" } ``` Reusable for dev, staging, prod with different settings.

5️⃣ Remote State (S3 + DynamoDB)

State local problem

By default, Terraform stores state in terraform.tfstate (local). Risks:
  • Loss of file = loss of state
  • No collaboration (conflicts)
  • No locking (2 people applying at the same time)

Solution: Remote State on S3

In backend.tf: ```hcl terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = "my-terraform-state" key = "prod/terraform.tfstate" region = "eu-west-1" dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks" encrypt = true } } ``` Advantages:
  • State shared between team
  • Versioning enabled (rollback possible)
  • Locking via DynamoDB (avoids conflicts)
  • Encrypted at rest

6️⃣ Workspaces (multi-environments)

Manage dev, staging, prod

  • terraform workspace new dev
  • terraform workspace new staging
  • terraform workspace new prod
  • terraform workspace select dev
Each workspace has its own state.

7️⃣ Terraform in the CI/CD

GitHub Actions example

```yaml name: Terraform on: [push] jobs: terraform: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v3 - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2 - run: terraform init - run: terraform plan ``` Automates terraform plan on each PR.

8️⃣ Best practices

  • ✅ Version your Terraform code (Git)
  • ✅ Remote state (S3 + DynamoDB or Terraform Cloud)
  • ✅ Reusable modules (DRY principle)
  • ✅ Variables for secrets (never hardcoded)
  • ✅ One workspace per environment
  • ✅ Always run plan before apply
  • ✅ Code review of infrastructure changes
  • ✅ Terraform fmt (automatic format)
  • ✅ Terraform validate (check syntax)

9️⃣ Terraform vs other tools

Terraform vs Ansible

  • Terraform: Provisioning infrastructure (create servers)
  • Ansible: Configuration management (configure existing servers)
Often used set: Terraform creates the infrastructure, Ansible configures it.

Terraform vs CloudFormation

  • Terraform: Multi-cloud, HCL (readable)
  • CloudFormation: AWS only, YAML/JSON (verbose)

🎯 Conclusion

Reliable Infrastructure = Infrastructure as Code! Key benefits:
  • Versioned as code
  • Reproducible
  • Testable
  • Automatically documented
  • Easy multi-environment
Resources:
  • developer.hashicorp.com/terraform
  • registry.terraform.io (official modules)
  • spacelift.io/blog (best practices)
> "Infrastructure as Code: because clicking buttons in the AWS console at 2 AM is not sustainable." 🏗️

title: DevOps Security: The Essentials (DevSecOps)
content:
Introduction: Shift Left Security

DevSecOps = Integrate security from the beginning of the development cycle, not at the end. Principle of "Shift Left": The earlier you detect a vulnerability, the less it costs to correct.

❌ Traditional approach

  • Dev → Test → Security audit at end of project
  • Vulnerabilities discovered just before the release
  • Panic, rush, last minute patches

✅ DevSecOps

  • Automated security in CI/CD
  • Vulnerability scanning at each commit
  • Immediate feedback for devs

1️⃣ Dependency Scan (SCA)

Issue: Vulnerable dependencies

80% of a modern app's code comes from external dependencies (npm, pip, Maven...). Example: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) affected millions of Java apps.

Scanning tools

  • npm audit: Integrated with npm
  • Snyk: Scan + auto-fix vulnerabilities
  • Dependabot (GitHub): Automatic PRs to update deps
  • OWASP Dependency-Check: Open source

CI/CD integration

In GitHub Actions: Pipeline fails if critical vulnerabilities detected.

2️⃣ Static Code Scan (SAST)

What is SAST?

Static Application Security Testing: Analyze your source code for flaws (without running it). Examples of vulnerabilities detected:
  • SQL Injection
  • XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
  • Hardcoded secrets (API keys in code)
  • Buffer overflow

SAST Tools

  • SonarQube: Open source, supports 25+ languages
  • Semgrep: Light, fast
  • CodeQL (GitHub): Free for public repositories
  • Checkmarx: Enterprise

3️⃣ Secret Scan

Problem: Committed secrets

Example of secrets to NEVER commit:
  • AWS Access Keys
  • API tokens (Stripe, SendGrid...)
  • Passwords
  • Private SSH keys

Detection tools

  • GitGuardian: Real-time scan of commits
  • TruffleHog: Git history scan
  • GitHub Secret Scanning: Native GitHub
  • git-secrets: Pre-commit hook

⚠️ If a secret has been committed

  • Immediately revoke key
  • Clean Git History (BFG Repo-Cleaner)
  • Force re-clone of repo for team

4️⃣ Scanning Docker images

Vulnerabilities in images

A Docker image may contain OS vulnerabilities (Ubuntu, Alpine...) or vulnerable packages.

Scanning tools

  • Trivy: Ultra-fast open source scanner
  • Snyk Container: Scan + recommendations
  • Docker Scout: Integrated with Docker Desktop
  • Clear: By CoreOS

Example with Trivy

  • trivy image nginx:latest
Shows all detected CVEs.

5️⃣ Infrastructure as Code Security

Scan Terraform/CloudFormation

Tools:
  • Checkov: Scanning Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes YAML
  • tfsec: Terraform specific
  • Terrascan: Multi-IaC
Examples of detections:
  • Bucket S3 public by mistake
  • Security group too permissive (0.0.0.0/0)
  • Encryption disabled

6️⃣ Secret management (Vault)

Secrets management solutions

  • HashiCorp Vault: Industry standard
  • AWS Secrets Manager: Native AWS
  • Azure Key Vault: Native Azure
  • Doppler: Simple and modern
  • Infisical: Open source alternative

Principle

  • Secrets stored encrypted in Vault
  • App retrieves secrets at runtime (not hardcoded)
  • Automatic secret rotation
  • Audit logs of all accesses

7️⃣ OWASP Top 10

The 10 critical web vulnerabilities

  • A01: Broken Access Control
  • A02: Cryptographic Failures (unencrypted data)
  • A03: Injection (SQL, NoSQL, LDAP...)
  • A04: Insecure Design (vulnerable architecture)
  • A05: Security Misconfiguration
  • A06: Vulnerable Components (dependencies)
  • A07: Authentication Failures
  • A08: Software and Data Integrity
  • A09: Logging Failures
  • A10: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

8️⃣ DevSecOps Best Practices

  • ✅ Automate scans in CI/CD
  • ✅ Fail fast: Pipeline blocked if critical vulnerability
  • ✅ Secret rotation (every 90 days)
  • ✅ Principle of least privilege (Minimum IAM)
  • ✅ Access monitoring (audit logs)
  • ✅ MFA everywhere (Multi-Factor Authentication)
  • ✅ Network segmentation (VPC, private subnets)
  • ✅ Patch management (regular updates)

🎯 Conclusion

Security is not a final step, it is a continuous process. The 3 DevSecOps pillars:
  • Automation (scans in CI/CD)
  • Visibility (vulnerability monitoring)
  • Responsiveness (quick patch)
